newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PNG's Chan says will fight again at ballot box.
newsitem.headline: PNG's Chan says will fight again at ballot box.

text.p: Sir Julius Chan, forced to step down as Papua New Guinea's prime minister by military and popular pressure, said on Thursday he would fight the next election in the South Pacific nation.
Chan, in a radio interview, refused to accept that his decision to go was a personal defeat or a victory for sacked army chief Jerry Singirok, who had demanded his resignation.

"I have not conceded on anything at all...The decision I made was entirely mine as the chief executive of this country and it's really between myself, my conscience and the effect on the population of this country. It's got nothing to do with Singirok whatsoever," Chan said.
"I've got no qualm at all standing for the election," he told Radio New Zealand.
Chan said he had won a 60 percent majority in his constituency at the last election. "I will, I hope, increase that majority," he said.
Papua New Guinea was plunged into turmoil after the military demanded Chan quit over a decision to hire foreign mercenaries to crush an ethnic uprising on the island of Bougainville.
Chan, 57, said on Wednesday he would "step aside" during an inquiry into the contract and ahead of elections in June.
In the interview, he said protests against him in the capital, Port Moresby, represented dissatisfaction among only a small percentage of the population.
"You know, the old saying goes, the silent majority don't speak out."
Chan was guarded in his comments about the hiring of 70 African mercenaries from British-based military consultancy Sandline International.

"We are dealing with a very classified matter... there are things that Singirok can say that I cannot, there are classified materials. The mere fact that they raise it, that we may have done something wrong, I have no problem at all with that... let the court rule.
"If I'm called (before the judicial inquiry) I'll go and produce whatever documents I need to," he said.
Asked if he would remain in Papua New Guinea, Chan said: "Where else can I go? Are you going to invite me to New Zealand or something?"
